evidence_quotes.quote: In houses where water is not installed, people either obtain it from wells dug in a putrid subsoil or they have to fetch it at a public fountain, so they save water in all possible ways.
Since most of the technical networks belonged to private companies, well-to-do consumers were favoured in order to assure returns on the big investments

The economic straits of the times also prevented the spread of water meters, as opposed to what was provided in the Municipal Health Regulations approved by Royal Decree in 1925. Despite the modest increase in water meters, trickle-feed contracts persisted and, since they covered entire tenement houses where the water was included in the rent, these contracts served to limit consumption severely.

In 1859, the municipal services made a complete inspection of all the cobbled pavements and sewers in Barcelona’s streets. Although 90 per cent of the streets had sewers, only 57 per cent of these were in good condition. In the working-class district of La Barceloneta, standing at a negligible height above sea level, 81 per cent of the streets lacked sewers.

Some urban areas were clearly excluded from the new services, above all in the peripheral working-class districts that arose in the 1920s and 1930s, where there was a very low level of urban development and very limited access to technical networks.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking-water supply and domestic sanitation/sewer connections in Barcelona from 1867 to 1967, including reliance on wells, public fountains, and bath-houses versus domestic piped water and flush sanitation.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, this paper clearly qualifies (plain_criterion2_decision = include) because it examines municipal water governance, failed municipalization attempts, private utility consolidation, municipal sanitary ordinances, and state decrees for river transfers. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, although substantial portions of the narrative trace hydraulic infrastructure delivery (elevation pumping, sewer renewal, and Llobregat/Ter surface-water transfers), the paper also directly examines rule-type and institutional mechanisms governing household access: (1) utility ownership and market structure (consolidation of private monopoly SGAB alongside failed municipalization, whereby private utilities prioritized central affluent areas for investment returns and left peripheral working-class districts unserved); (2) upfront concession and connection cost-recovery rules (municipal ploma fees plus costly house piping works); and (3) metering regulations and landlord-utility contracting rules (non-spread of compulsory water meters despite the Municipal Health Regulations approved by Royal Decree in 1925, and persistence of landlord trickle-feed contracts bundled into tenement rent that severely restricted tenants' water supply, alongside the 1891 municipal ordinances regulating continuous-circulation sewer connections and flush toilets). Thus it satisfies Criterion 2 under both readings.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary archival empirical evidence and descriptive quantitative historical time series compiled from municipal archives (AMCB, AHCB), utility company archives (Fundacion AGBAR Fonds, including SGAB water distribution and subscriber curves for 1910-1945 in Figure 1 and supply provenance series for 1950-1974 in Figure 2), 1859 municipal sewer inspection records, and historical price catalogues, rather than pure commentary or doctrinal essay.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple service access outcomes: household piped connection and subscriber growth, domestic per-capita and total water consumption, spatial exclusion of working-class and peripheral districts (continued reliance on wells and public fountains), sewer coverage across streets/districts, and service continuity restrictions (e.g., 30% service-hour cuts in May 1953).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (households, tenement buildings, urban districts, and utility system in Barcelona, Spain), exposure (private utility monopoly ownership structure, connection cost rules, 1891/1925 sanitary and metering regulations, and tenement trickle-feed supply contracts alongside bulk supply expansion), outcome (domestic connection, water quantity consumed, spatial exclusion, and continuity), and study design (longitudinal archival historical case study) are all identifiable from the text.

study_design: Longitudinal archival historical case study (combining primary municipal and utility archival documents with descriptive historical time-series data).
population_and_sample: Households, tenement buildings, and urban districts of Barcelona, Spain (1867-1967; city population growing from c. 600,000 in 1914 to over 1,000,000 in 1930), plus utility-level records of Sociedad General de Aguas de Barcelona (SGAB) and municipal systems.
exposure: Private utility monopoly ownership structure (SGAB consolidation vs. failed municipalization), upfront concession/connection cost rules, municipal sanitary and metering regulations (1891 continuous-circulation ordinances; 1925 Royal Decree Municipal Health Regulations), and tenement landlord trickle-feed vs. metered supply contracts (alongside hydraulic supply expansion).
outcome: Household piped water and sewer connection, per-capita and aggregate domestic water consumption, spatial exclusion of working-class and peripheral urban districts (continued reliance on wells, public fountains, and bath-houses), and service-hour supply restrictions.
rationale: This archival urban-history case study examines the 1867-1967 transition of Barcelona's domestic drinking-water and sanitation systems using primary municipal and utility archival records and quantitative historical supply/consumption series. Although framed broadly around long-term infrastructural modernization, it substantively analyzes rule-type institutional and regulatory mechanisms directly governing household access under Criterion 2 (both plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings): private utility monopoly ownership (SGAB) favoring affluent central districts and excluding peripheral working-class areas, upfront concession/piping costs, 1891 sewer/toilet ordinances, and tenement landlords' persistence with rent-bundled trickle-feed contracts rather than individual meters despite the 1925 Royal Decree Municipal Health Regulations. Confidence is medium because the study follows a narrative historiographical format without a standalone social-science methods section and intertwines institutional/contractual mechanisms with bulk hydraulic engineering expansion.
